items.question: What is JRE?
items.answer: Answer: JRE stands for Java Runtime Environment. It is the environment in which a Java program is loaded and executed. One way to understand it is as the region in RAM used for running a Java application.

items.question: Why does a Java program need a runtime environment?
items.answer: Answer: A Java program cannot simply be loaded anywhere in memory and executed. The operating system allocates a specific region in RAM where the Java program and the required execution-related components are loaded.

items.question: Does every running Java application use its own runtime environment?
items.answer: Answer: Yes. Each Java application gets its own runtime environment for execution. For example, if two Java applications are running, each application has its own allocated execution environment.

items.question: What is another way to define JRE?
items.answer: Answer: JRE can also be described as a collection of software required to execute a Java program. Important components discussed include: JVM Java libraries Class loader Bytecode verifier

items.question: What is JVM?
items.answer: Answer: JVM stands for Java Virtual Machine. It is responsible for executing Java bytecode by providing the required execution mechanisms.

items.question: What important components are present inside the JVM?
items.answer: Answer: Important components discussed include: JIT compiler Java interpreter Runtime system These components participate in Java program execution.

items.question: What is JIT?
items.answer: Answer: JIT stands for Just-In-Time Compiler. It converts Java bytecode into machine-level instructions during execution.

items.question: What is the role of the Java interpreter?
items.answer: Answer: The Java interpreter also participates in converting or executing bytecode. Both the interpreter and JIT are involved in converting bytecode into a form that can ultimately be executed by the machine.

items.question: What is the difference between JIT and the Java interpreter at this level?
items.answer: Answer: Both are involved in handling bytecode and machine-level execution, but they perform that work differently. The main distinction is when and how the conversion happens.

items.question: What is the purpose of the runtime system inside the JVM?
items.answer: Answer: The runtime system supports activities required while the Java program is executing. Exception-handling support is given as one example of runtime responsibility.

items.question: What is a class loader?
items.answer: Answer: A class loader is a component required during Java execution to load the classes needed by the program. It is one of the important components used when a Java application runs.

items.question: What is a bytecode verifier?
items.answer: Answer: A bytecode verifier checks whether the bytecode is valid Java bytecode and whether it has been improperly modified. This verification contributes to Java's security.

items.question: What are Java libraries?
items.answer: Answer: Java libraries contain predefined functionality that Java programs can use. Required library code is made available during program execution.

items.question: What is JDK?
items.answer: Answer: JDK stands for Java Development Kit. It is a toolkit containing the software required to: Write Java programs Compile Java programs Execute Java programs

items.question: Why is it called a Development Kit?
items.answer: Answer: Java development involves activities such as: Writing Compiling Executing The JDK bundles the tools required to perform these development activities.

items.question: What is the difference between JDK, JRE, JVM, and JIT?
items.answer: Answer: JDK → Toolkit used to develop, compile, and execute Java programs. JRE → Environment required to run a Java program. JVM → Execution system responsible for running Java bytecode. JIT → Compiler inside the JVM that converts bytecode into machine-level code during execution.

items.question: What is the basic Java execution flow?
items.answer: Answer: Java Source Code ↓ Java Compiler ↓ Bytecode (.class file) ↓ JVM ↓ JIT / Interpreter ↓ Machine-Level Instructions ↓ Execution

items.question: What happens when a Java source file is compiled?
items.answer: Answer: The Java compiler converts the source code into bytecode and stores it in a .class file. The .class file is not called an object file here; it is specifically referred to as a class file.

items.question: What command is used to compile a Java source file?
items.answer: Answer: The Java compiler command is: javac Example: javac Greet.java The compiler generates the corresponding .class file.

items.question: What command is used to execute a compiled Java class?
items.answer: Answer: The java command is used. Example: java Greet This starts execution of the compiled Java program.

items.question: What is the difference between System.out.print() and System.out.println()?
items.answer: Answer: print() prints the data and keeps the cursor on the same line. println() prints the data and then moves the cursor to the next line.

items.question: What does “Write Once, Run Anywhere” mean in Java?
items.answer: Answer: It means a Java program written and compiled once can run on different systems, provided the required Java execution environment is available. The same program can run irrespective of geographical location, operating-system platform, or system architecture.

items.question: Why can the same Java program run on different operating systems?
items.answer: Answer: Java source code is compiled into platform-independent bytecode. Each operating system uses the JVM appropriate for that platform to execute the bytecode.

items.question: Is the JVM platform independent?
items.answer: Answer: No. The Java language and bytecode are platform independent, but the JVM is platform dependent. Different platforms require their corresponding JVM implementations. Examples: Windows → Windows JVM Unix → Unix JVM macOS → macOS JVM

items.question: What does architecture-neutral mean in Java?
items.answer: Answer: Architecture-neutral means the same Java program can execute on machines with different underlying architectures without changing the program, provided the required JVM is available. The program behaves consistently irrespective of the architecture of the system on which it runs.

items.question: What does portability mean in Java?
items.answer: Answer: Portability means a Java program created on one platform can be transported to another platform and executed there. Program on Platform A ↓ Transport ↓ Platform B ↓ Execute This is why Java is described as a portable programming language.
